passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of caffeine on cognitive performance in a randomized controlled trial. 120 healthy adults aged 18‑35 were assigned to four groups: placebo, 50 mg caffeine, 100 mg caffeine, and 200 mg caffeine. Each participant completed a 30‑minute Stroop task after ingesting their assigned beverage. Response times and error rates were recorded. Table 1 summarizes the mean response times and standard deviations for each group. The study aimed to determine whether increasing caffeine dosage leads to a linear improvement in reaction speed and whether there is a threshold beyond which performance declines. The authors also collected subjective alertness ratings on a 10‑point Likert scale. Data analysis involved one-way ANOVA with post‑hoc Tukey tests. The researchers hypothesized that 100 mg caffeine would yield the fastest responses, while 200 mg might produce fatigue effects. Results indicated a significant main effect of dose (p < .01), with 100 mg outperforming placebo (p < .001) and 200 mg not significantly different from placebo. The authors concluded that moderate caffeine improves cognitive speed, but higher doses do not confer additional benefits and the 200 mg dose was no better than placebo.
stem: According to Table 1, which caffeine dose group had the fastest mean response time?
explanation: The 100 mg group had the lowest mean response time (590 ms), indicating the fastest performance.
trap: Students may pick the 200 mg group because more caffeine seems faster, but its mean (640 ms) is slower than the 100 mg group (590 ms).

stem: Each participant received only one of the four beverages. Which design feature does this describe?
explanation: Correct: Participants were randomly assigned to one dose group and each experienced one condition only, which is a between-subjects design. Why the others are wrong: B) In a within-subjects design every participant receives every dose. C) There is more than one group and no pre-post comparison of a single group. D) Case-control studies compare people grouped by outcome, not randomly assigned exposure.
trap: Students see several groups and a repeated task and call it within-subjects, but each person was in only one caffeine condition.

stem: If the standard error of the mean for the 100 mg group is calculated as SD/√n, where n = 30, what is the approximate standard error?
trap: Students divide by n = 30 without taking the square root, or by n/2, giving 2.33 or 4.67 instead of 12.78 ms.

stem: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the study's findings?

options.A: 200 mg caffeine improves performance more than 100 mg
options.B: 100 mg caffeine improves performance compared to placebo
options.C: The 100 mg group had a lower mean response time than the 200 mg group
options.D: 200 mg caffeine has similar performance to placebo

explanation: Correct: The 200 mg group (640 ms) was slower than the 100 mg group (590 ms) and not different from placebo, so it did not improve performance more than 100 mg. Why the others are wrong: B) 100 mg outperformed placebo (p < .001). C) 590 ms is lower than 640 ms. D) 200 mg did not differ significantly from placebo.
trap: Students assume more caffeine means better performance (a linear dose-response), but the 200 mg group was no better than placebo and slower than 100 mg.

stem: Which of the following best links the study's findings to broader implications for caffeine consumption guidelines?

options.A: Moderate caffeine improved cognitive speed, and the higher dose gave no additional benefit.
options.B: Caffeine has no effect on cognition.
options.D: Caffeine is harmful at all doses.

explanation: Correct: 100 mg improved response time versus placebo while 200 mg did not differ from placebo, supporting moderate dosing. Why the others are wrong: B) 100 mg clearly improved performance. C) The high dose did not improve performance. D) No dose slowed responses relative to placebo.
trap: Students choose 'only high doses improve cognition' because they expect a larger dose to give a larger effect, but the 200 mg group did not improve.
